Supporting passages also verbatim: sec. 37 (line 1042-1043) 'a form of demonstrative, which pronounced with stress on the first syllable expresses an emphatic negative'; sec. 38 (line 1048) 'used without stress as a weak demonstrative' in Wisa; s…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for 'Lala and Wisa' has an empty rule field; this is the first placement statement found for lala1264: penultimate (usual), with antepenultimate stress also common. Describes the south-western (Lala-Lamba) division of the Wisa-Lala dialect; the accent sentence covers Lala and Wisa jointly.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent normally falls on the penultimate syllable in both Lala and Wisa; an antepenultimate stress is also described as 'very common'. Madan's accent is a stress notion (he uses 'accent' and 'stress' interchangeably); no tone is mentioned.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated as such; the 'very commonly' antepenultimate stress alongside the usual penult may be a second prominence rather than an alternative placement, but the text does not say.
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenultimate stress 'very commonly' (p. 11 sec. 9). Grammatical stress: a demonstrative 'pronounced with stress on the first syllable expresses an emphatic negative' (sec. 37), used 'without stress as a weak demonstrative' in Wisa (sec. 38); in the perfect-definite use of the -a- tense 'a stress is often laid on the tense-sign, a' (sec. 75).
new_statements.identity_note: Madan 1908 covers the south-western division of the Wisa-Lala dialect (what he calls Lala-Lamba) of Northern Rhodesia, and states the accent rule for 'Lala and Wisa' together. Madan 1914 treats Lala of the district around Livingstone's death place (Chitambo area) and adjacent Northern Rhodesia / Belgian Congo, contrasting it with Lamba (west) and Wisa (east). Collard 1920 (not opened) describes Lala-Lamba as spoken from Sakania to Elisabethville, i.e. the Katanga (Lamba-leaning) side.

audit.reasoning: Quote check passes on all three copies we hold at the stated locators. The classification (tonal, no word-stress rule; impressionistic penult accent with frequent antepenult stress as secondary) rests on two 1906/1908 missionary handbooks plus a 1978 Zambia-wide survey chapter that presents no Lala-Bisa data, so the evidence is old and partly second-hand, but nothing located contradicts it: Glottolog (Glottolog's most extensive description = Madan 1906; 57 language refs, 105 family-node refs), Grambank (source = Madan 1906), the UNZA repository and Semantic Scholar show no grammar, phonology, tone or instrumental study of Lala-Bisa. No open source could be downloaded (search engines blocked, budgets exhausted; one the Internet Archive PDF turned out to be a mislinked unrelated article and was discarded). The only modern prosodic analysis nearby is Bickmore 1995 on Lamba, a distinct sister languoid, which could inform but not reclassify this record. Henc
